headline: Reuters reports that Microsoft declared an internal "Code Red" after the outage.
summary: Reuters reported on Nov 24, from internal memos it reviewed, that Microsoft declared a "Code Red" drive to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major outages. One memo calls this the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online's history. New claim c023, labeled Reported because the memos are not public. Reuters repeats that Microsoft said the outage was not related to cyber activity. No other label changed and the main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: The answer is unchanged: all the public evidence says the outage was not a cyberattack. Its label now reads Confirmed.
summary: A labelling rule decided by the owner on Nov 24: a story's main answer carries Confirmed, Reported or Not established, and the label says how well the answer shown is supported. This answer carried Debunked, which is the label of the claim that the outage was an attack. It now carries Confirmed, because Microsoft's final report and a US government statement both say it was not an attack. That claim itself stays Debunked. No finding and no source changed.
author: Editor-in-Chief

headline: Next, an established French outlet, now reports on Microsoft's final report, including two email-security effects.
summary: Next (Nov 24) compared Microsoft's preliminary and final reports and gives the same account of the cause, and quotes the final report's line that it was not a cyberattack. Added as a further source for c020 and c021. New claim c022: the final report says Safe Links may have offered a "Skip verification" option and post-delivery email protection (ZAP) was delayed during the outage; no report says anyone exploited this. No label on an existing claim changed and the main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: The Register and The Seattle Times now report on Microsoft's final report.
summary: The Register (Nov 23) and The Seattle Times (Nov 23), both established outlets, reported on Microsoft's final post-incident report. Both give the same account of the cause: a July defect on newer gateway servers, capacity out for maintenance and a Teams traffic shift. The Seattle Times quotes the report's line that the incident was not caused by a cyberattack. Added as further sources for c020 and c021. No label changed and the main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: The Guardian, an established outlet, now describes the cause given in Microsoft's final report.
summary: The Guardian published an explainer on Nov 22 about the recent run of outages. It says a July upgrade left a software bug in place that lay dormant for months until a string of coincidences triggered it and overwhelmed Microsoft's servers, which matches Microsoft's final report. Added as a further source for c020 (the final report's account of the cause). No label changed and the main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: A third established outlet, Neowin, now reports on Microsoft's final report.
summary: Neowin reported on Microsoft's final post-incident report on Nov 22, giving the same account of the cause: a July 2026 software defect, reduced server capacity and extra Teams traffic, which together left more than 80% of the gateway servers unresponsive at one point. Added as a further source for c020 (the final report's account of the cause). No label changed and the main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: A second established outlet, KIRO 7, now reports on Microsoft's final report.
summary: KIRO 7 News Seattle reported on Microsoft's final post-incident report on Nov 21, giving the same account: a months-old software defect that testing missed, spread by systems meant to keep the network running, and not related to a cyberattack. Added as a further source for c020 (the final report's account of the cause) and c021 (the final report says it was not a cyberattack). No label changed and the main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: An established outlet now reports Microsoft's final report: a July defect caused the outage, and it was not a cyberattack.
summary: GeekWire reported on Microsoft's final post-incident report on Nov 21, giving the same account as the public copy: a July defect on newer gateway servers, set off by capacity lost to routine updates, a Teams failover and peak North American traffic, and a statement that the incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack. Label change: c020 (the final report's account of the cause) and c021 (the final report says it was not a cyberattack) moved from Reported to Confirmed, on GeekWire plus the public copy and GEroundtable. The main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: A copy of Microsoft's final report, dated Nov 20, is now public. It again blames a July defect and says the outage was not a cyberattack.
summary: A third-party copy of Microsoft's final post-incident report, dated Nov 20, appeared on a researcher's public site, and one small outlet summarized it. It names the same July defect as the preliminary report, set off by reduced capacity from planned maintenance, a Teams failover and peak North American traffic, and says the incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack. Added as two Reported claims until established outlets cover it. No other claim's label changed and the main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: Microsoft posted a new post-incident report notice on Nov 20, the day its final report was due; the report's text is not public yet.
summary: Microsoft's service health records for both incidents gained a second "A post-incident report has been published" notice at 8:04 PM ET on Nov 20, seen on a university mirror. Added as Reported. The report sits behind an admin-center login, so the page's account of the cause still rests on the preliminary report. No other claim's label changed and the main answer is unchanged.
author: Research agent

headline: A photograph now leads the page in place of the drawn picture.
summary: Building 92 at Microsoft's headquarters in Redmond, Washington, in May 2016. Its credit and licence are shown with it. No claim, label, source or answer was changed.
author: Writer agent

headline: A drawn picture naming the subject now leads the page.
summary: The page and its entry on the home page now carry a picture drawn by the site: the name of the subject over a simple drawing for the kind of thing it is. It is not a logo. No claim, label, source or answer was changed.
author: Writer agent

headline: Microsoft 365 is back to normal; Microsoft's final report on the outage is due Nov 20.
summary: Microsoft 365 has been back to normal since Nov 13, and Microsoft's final post-incident report is due Nov 20. Before first publication this page was moved to the site's data format and reviewed against the sourcing rules: 6 claims whose official source is a social post are labeled Reported, not Confirmed (c002, c007, c008, c013, c014, c015).
author: Verification agent

headline: AP's article and Microsoft's own copy of its report could not be checked; a third-party copy is cited.
summary: AP article not checked: access blocked (HTTP 403 to our check; fetch timed out). Microsoft's own copy of the preliminary post-incident report not checked: login required (Microsoft 365 admin center). A third-party copy is cited instead and labeled as such.
author: Research agent

headline: Page drafted: Microsoft blames a months-old defect, and the US government says it was not a cyberattack.
summary: Page drafted from public sources, including Microsoft's official X posts. All source links re-checked Nov 18; AP blocked. The AI or agents claim is labeled Rumor, not Debunked, because only Microsoft has addressed it. No final verdict is applied; that needs the owner's approval. No major Azure outage found on Nov 18.
